Table 8. Step card – Grouped, stratified 70:30 hold-out validation (Steps F1–F3).
rows: The 48 plots are divided once into a training set (about 70% of the leaves) and a test set (about 30%). Every step that learns from the data – feature selection, model choice, tuning and training – uses the training plots only; the test plots are used once, at the end, to measure accuracy.

Leaves of one plot share soil, microclimate and inoculum, so a random split of leaves would put near-copies of the same plot in training and test and inflate accuracy; whole plots are therefore assigned to one side only (Roberts et al., 2017). Stratification keeps the test set representative: healthy (sprayed) and unsprayed plots are split separately, the unsprayed test plots come from different treatments and are spread evenly over replications, varieties and sowing timings, and among 5000 candidate splits the one closest to 30% of the leaves and to the overall grade and date distribution was chosen (Kuhn and Johnson, 2013). 70:30 is a common hold-out ratio (Gholamy et al., 2018; Joseph, 2022).

Hold-out (train/test) validation with stratified splitting (Kuhn and Johnson, 2013); grouped or blocked splitting of dependent samples (Roberts et al., 2017); selection and tuning inside the training set only, to avoid selection bias (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002; Varma and Simon, 2006; Cawley and Talbot, 2010); hold-out vs cross-validation with small samples (Kohavi, 1995; Vabalas et al., 2019).

Test plots: healthy 1, 4, 5, 8; unsprayed R1 37, 44, 46, 48, R2 25, 27, 31, 35, R3 13, 14, 18 (11 different treatments). 699 test leaves (30.0%) and 1631 training leaves from 33 plots. Feature selection, SFFS and grid search use only the training plots, with inner GroupKFold(3) by plot; the networks stop early on one third of the training plots. The split is reproducible (seed 2026, split_lib.py).

Test predictions of the 699 test leaves for every model. With one test set there are no folds: the uncertainty of each metric comes from a plot bootstrap of the test set (1000 resamples of whole test plots, healthy and unsprayed plots separately; Efron and Tibshirani, 1993; Field and Welsh, 2007).

LORO (the earlier analysis) tested every leaf once and pooled three folds. Chapter 4 compares the two designs on the same test leaves and over 20 other 70:30 splits. Leave-one-date-out was not used because the dates differ in growth stage and disease level (see 2.12 for the transfer tests).

caption: Table 12. Step card – Spectral range, smoothing and first derivative.
rows: Spectral range, smoothing and first derivative

Savitzky–Golay smoothing fits a local polynomial in a moving window; the same fit gives the first derivative, which removes additive offsets and sharpens the red edge (Savitzky and Golay, 1964; Tsai and Philpot, 1998).

Contact-probe spectra are clean, but the detector ends (350–399 nm and 2401–2500 nm) are noisy. Water-absorption regions (1350–1460 and 1790–1960 nm) were kept: the probe uses its own light source, so atmospheric water does not affect them, and they carry leaf-water information.
Savitzky–Golay with the first derivative in rice blast (Ma et al., 2026) and wheat diseases (Huang et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2020); derivative analysis of leaf spectra (Tsai and Philpot, 1998).

Savitzky–Golay window 11 nm, order 2, applied on 350–2500 nm; spectra trimmed to 400–2400 nm; first derivative from the same filter; bands taken every 5 nm (401 reflectance + 401 derivative features).
Smoothed reflectance Rλ and first derivative FDλ (×10-3 nm-1) at 5 nm.
The second derivative was not used (agreed rule: it amplifies noise). Standard normal variate and continuum removal were not needed for contact-probe data.

caption: Table 13. Vegetation indices and red-edge parameters computed for every leaf, with Pearson r against the leaf grade (n = 2330).
rows: wavelength of maximum FD in 680–760 nm

caption: Table 14. Step card – Activity 1.1 – Response analysis.
rows: Mean reflectance and first-derivative curves of each grade show where and how the spectrum changes with disease; Pearson correlation of each band with the grade measures the strength of the change.
It is the first, model-free evidence of the disease signal and shows whether the response is consistent across varieties, stages and dates.
Mean spectra and correlation curves are the standard first step in disease spectroscopy (Mahlein et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2020; Mandal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2026).
Means ± SD by grade for 400–2400 nm; first derivative; r of each 5-nm band and derivative with the grade; spectra by growth stage; mean grade by stage, variety, leaf position and timing.
Disease-sensitive regions; evidence for the band selection that follows.

caption: Table 15. Step card – Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS).
rows: Activity 1.2 – Effective ranges and optimal wavelengths (SHAP-CARS)

NDSI and RSI are computed for every pair of bands; the R² with the grade forms a map whose high-value area defines the effective wavelength ranges. Inside them, a gradient-boosting model ranks bands by mean |SHAP| (top 40% kept) and CARS with PLS selects the final optimal wavelengths.
802 correlated bands cannot go into a model directly. SHAP removes uninformative bands before CARS, so CARS works on a smaller, relevant set and is more stable (Ma et al., 2026).
NDSI/RSI R² maps and SHAP-CARS for rice blast (Ma et al., 2026); CARS (Li et al., 2009); SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020).

Threshold R² ≥ 0.5 for effective ranges, else the top 5% of pairs (used here: R² ≥ 0.228); red-edge derivatives 680–760 nm always candidates; XGBoost (300 trees, depth 4, learning rate 0.05); bands standardised; PLS components by Monte Carlo cross-validation (50 splits); CARS 50 iterations × 20 runs; bands kept if selected in ≥ 50% of runs (maximum 15).
Reflectance and derivative bands were pooled in one SHAP-CARS run (agreed decision).

caption: Table 16. Step card – Activities 1.3–1.4 – Index construction and ReliefF selection.
rows: Activities 1.3–1.4 – Index construction and ReliefF selection

The best NDSI and RSI pairs come from the maps; the White Rust Index adds a third band to the best NDSI: WRI = NDSI(λ1, λ2) + w·Rλ3. Indices with |r| ≥ 0.95 are reduced to the one most correlated with the grade; ReliefF (classes) and RReliefF (score) rank the rest.

A three-band index can correct a confounding effect that a two-band index cannot; ReliefF judges an index by how well it separates near neighbours of different classes, so it handles interactions and is not fooled by correlation alone.

Three-band disease indices (Meng et al., 2020; Mandal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2026); ReliefF and RReliefF (Kira and Rendell, 1992; Kononenko, 1994; Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003; Urbanowicz et al., 2018).

WRI search: the 200 best NDSI pairs at least 50 nm apart, λ3 every 10 nm, w ∈ {−1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1}. ReliefF with k = 10 neighbours, neighbours from the same plot excluded; top five indices kept for each task.
Selected indices (VI) for detection, six grades and score.

caption: Table 17. Step card – Activity 1.6 – Variance inflation factor and the disease-specific feature set.
rows: Activity 1.6 – Variance inflation factor and the disease-specific feature set
VIF = 1/(1 − R²j) measures how well feature j is explained by the others; the feature with the largest VIF is removed until all are below 10.
Optimal wavelengths and indices overlap; strong collinearity makes models unstable and explanations unreliable (Dormann et al., 2013; O'Brien, 2007).
VIF screening before modelling (Dormann et al., 2013; Mandal et al., 2023).
Pool = optimal wavelengths + selected indices; iterative removal until all VIF < 10.
Disease-specific feature set (DSF): the input of Objective 2.

rows: DNN-F1 is a fully connected network on the feature vector. The other networks need images, so the p selected features were placed in a k × k pseudo-image (k = ⌈√p⌉, zero-padded). DT-EDNet is the network proposed for early rice-blast detection; EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18 and ConvNeXt V2 are the comparison networks of the same study, so the comparison follows the paper.

Table 36. Step card – Comparing two validation designs on the same data.
rows: Comparing two validation designs on the same data

A validation design is a way to estimate how accurate a model will be on new plots. LORO trains on two replications and tests on the third, three times, so every leaf is tested once; the 70:30 hold-out trains once on 70% of the plots and tests once on the other 30%. Both keep whole plots apart, so both are free of plot leakage.

A hold-out estimate depends on which plots happen to be in the test set, and with few test plots its variance is large; cross-validation averages over several test sets and uses every sample for testing (Kohavi, 1995; Molinaro et al., 2005; Vabalas et al., 2019; Xu and Goodacre, 2018). A higher 70:30 number is therefore an improvement only if it holds on the same leaves and across other 70:30 splits, not only for one lucky split.

Hold-out vs cross-validation for accuracy estimation (Kohavi, 1995; Molinaro et al., 2005); small-sample bias of single splits (Vabalas et al., 2019); split ratios (Dobbin and Simon, 2011; Xu and Goodacre, 2018; Joseph, 2022); leakage from non-independent samples (Roberts et al., 2017; Kapoor and Narayanan, 2023); plot (cluster) bootstrap (Field and Welsh, 2007).

(1) All metrics side by side: LORO (earlier analysis) vs 70:30. (2) Same test leaves: the LORO predictions of exactly the 70:30 test leaves (each leaf was tested once in LORO) vs the 70:30 predictions; difference with a 95% plot-bootstrap interval (2000 resamples of the test plots). (3) Split-to-split variability: a light, identical pipeline (selection on the training part, best ML model per task, grid search; no SFFS) run on LORO, on the main 70:30 split and on 20 other rule-conforming 70:30 splits. (4) Leakage check: the same light pipeline on 5 random 70:30 splits of leaves that ignore plots.
Answer to the question "does 70:30 improve accuracy?" with its evidence.
The 80:20 and 70:30 splits are compared with LORO in the same way; the separate comparison report puts all three side by side.
